chunks: LPF, HPF and BPF analysis basics. The question: Basic LPF/BPF/HPF filter analysis.
A filter lets some frequencies through and blocks others. A low-pass filter (LPF) passes slow signals and blocks fast ones. A high-pass filter (HPF) does the opposite.
A band-pass filter (BPF) passes only a middle range. A resistor and capacitor can build the simplest ones, because a capacitor's behavior changes with frequency.
Think of a car's suspension driving down a road. It smooths out quick, small bumps but follows the slow rise and fall of the hills. That is a low-pass filter.
A high-pass filter would be the reverse: it would ignore the hills and react only to the quick bumps.
Both are really just a voltage divider ("Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation") whose bottom or top part changes with frequency.
Same two parts, swapped positions. In the LPF, the output is across the capacitor, which shorts high frequencies to ground.
In the HPF, the capacitor sits in the signal path and blocks DC, so only changes get through.
Frequency: how many cycles per second a signal repeats, in hertz (Hz). Corner (cutoff) frequency: the point where the output has fallen to 0. 707 of the input.
For an RC filter, f c equals 1 over (2 pi RC) . Capacitor: a part that stores charge. It blocks steady, one-direction (DC) current but passes fast changes.
and "Capacitor impedance equation". dB (decibel): a way to say how much a signal shrinks. minus 3 decibels is about 0. 707 of the input, and minus 20 decibels is one tenth.
Roll-off: how steeply the output falls past the corner, here 20 decibels (ten times smaller) per tenfold rise in frequency.
Build a low-pass with a 1 kilohms resistor in series and a 159 nanofarads capacitor to ground.
Then f c equals 1 over (2 pi times 1000 times 159 times 10 to the -9) , about 1 kilohertz. At 100 hertz almost everything passes. At 1 kilohertz the output is 0. 707 of the input.
At 10 kilohertz it is only about 10%. That is the whole idea.
